questions.corrige_markdown:
**Astrogeology** is the study of the geology of the Moon, the planets and other bodies of the Solar System and of the Universe in which the Earth is set. The five terms are defined as follows.

**(i) Planets.** A planet is a large, nearly spherical body that **orbits a star** (for us, the Sun), is massive enough for its own gravity to have pulled it into a round shape, and has **cleared the neighbourhood of its orbit** of other debris. It has no light of its own and shines by **reflected sunlight**. There are eight planets in the Solar System: the small, rocky, dense **terrestrial (inner) planets** Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, and the large, gaseous or icy **giant (outer) planets** Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

**(ii) Galaxy.** A galaxy is an enormous, **gravitationally bound system of billions of stars**, together with gas, dust and dark matter, that revolves about a common centre. Galaxies are classed by shape as spiral, elliptical and irregular. Our Solar System lies in a spiral galaxy called the **Milky Way**, and the Universe contains billions of galaxies separated by very large distances.

**(iii) Nebula (nebular).** A nebula is a **vast interstellar cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen and helium) and dust**. Some nebulae are the **birth places of stars**, because the cloud contracts under gravity and heats up (the Orion Nebula), and others are the remains of dying or exploded stars (planetary nebulae and supernova remnants). In the *nebular hypothesis* the Sun and the planets formed from a rotating cloud of this kind, the solar nebula, about 4.6 billion years ago.

**(iv) Maria.** *Maria* (singular *mare*, Latin for "sea") are the **dark, smooth, low-lying plains of the Moon**. They are huge impact basins that were later flooded by **basaltic lava**, which is rich in iron and magnesium and is therefore dark, and they are younger (about 3 to 4 billion years old) and less cratered than the bright, rugged lunar highlands. Examples are Mare Imbrium and Mare Tranquillitatis. Early observers thought that they were seas of water.

**(v) Meteors.** A meteor is the **streak of light ("shooting star")** produced when a small solid particle from space, a **meteoroid**, enters the Earth's atmosphere at very high speed and is heated to incandescence by friction and compression of the air, so that it glows and usually burns up. A meteoroid that survives and reaches the ground is called a **meteorite** (stony, iron or stony-iron).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) On the world map provided, mark and label the distribution of the major belts of earthquakes.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**What the candidate must draw.** The earthquakes of the world are not scattered at random but are concentrated in narrow **belts**, which follow the boundaries of the lithospheric plates. On the outline map the candidate should draw each belt as a shaded or hatched band, give it a letter or number, and write the name of the belt in a key (labelled map = labelled belts, with a title). The five marks are earned by the belts below.

1. **The Circum-Pacific Belt (the "Ring of Fire")** is the most important belt, with about 80 per cent of the world's earthquakes. It surrounds the Pacific Ocean: along the west coast of South America (the Andes, from Chile to Colombia), through Central America and Mexico, the west coast of North America (California and Alaska), the Aleutian Islands, Kamchatka, the Kuril Islands, Japan, Taiwan, the Philippines, Indonesia (partly), New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Kermadec and New Zealand. It is a belt of **subduction zones** (deep-focus and shallow earthquakes) with the transform San Andreas Fault. On the map it is a band that goes round the edge of the Pacific Ocean from Chile to New Zealand.
2. **The Alpine-Himalayan (Mediterranean-Trans-Asiatic) Belt** has about 15 per cent of the earthquakes. It runs **east to west** from the Atlantic (the Azores and Portugal), along the Mediterranean (Morocco and Algeria, Italy, the Balkans, Greece), Turkey, Iran, Afghanistan, the Himalayas and Myanmar, and joins the Circum-Pacific Belt in Indonesia. It marks **continental collision** zones.
3. **The Mid-Oceanic Ridge Belt.** A narrow, continuous band along the crest of the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** (from Iceland southwards to near Antarctica), the Mid-Indian Ocean Ridge and the East Pacific Rise. The earthquakes are **shallow and of small magnitude**, and are due to the tension and the transform faults at the **divergent (constructive) boundaries**.
4. **The East African Rift System (continental rift belt)**, from the Afar region and the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden through Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania and Malawi towards Mozambique. It is a belt of shallow earthquakes in a **continental rift** valley where Africa is splitting.

**Labelling.** The belts should be labelled directly (for example "Circum-Pacific Belt", "Alpine-Himalayan Belt", "Mid-Atlantic Ridge belt", "East African Rift"), and the plate boundary type (subduction, collision, divergent) may be added. A good map also shows the distribution of the **epicentres as dots** in these bands and an **empty area** in the stable continental interiors, such as the African shield, the Brazilian shield and Australia, to illustrate that these areas have few earthquakes. The part of the map inside Cameroon (a stable shield area, with the weak seismicity of the Cameroon Volcanic Line) has no major belt.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Describe FIVE syndepositional sedimentary structures.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Syndepositional sedimentary structures** (primary sedimentary structures) are structures that are formed **at the time of deposition of the sediment**, or immediately after, as a result of the way the sediment was laid down (current, waves, gravity). They are used to find the **way up** of a bed, the direction of the current and the environment of deposition. Five of them are described.

1. **Graded bedding.** A bed in which the **grain size changes gradually from the base to the top**, normally from coarse at the base to fine at the top (normal grading), as the larger and heavier grains settle first when a current loses energy. It is typical of **turbidity currents** (turbidites) and of floods. The base of the bed is sharp, and the top passes gradually into the finer bed above. It shows the way up.
2. **Cross-bedding (cross-stratification).** Sets of inclined laminae, **at an angle to the main bedding planes**, formed by the migration of **ripples, sand waves, dunes or deltaic fronts**. The laminae dip in the direction of the current flow (the downstream side), and are truncated at the top by erosion and at the base they are tangential. They are found in river channel sands, desert dune sands (large-scale) and tidal environments, and they show the **palaeocurrent direction**.
3. **Ripple marks.** Small ridges and troughs on the surface of a bed of sand. **Current ripples** are **asymmetrical** (a gentle upstream slope and a steep downstream slope) and are formed by a one-direction current (a river); **wave (oscillation) ripples** are **symmetrical** with sharp crests and rounded troughs and are formed by waves in shallow water. They indicate the direction of flow or the shallow-water environment, and they show the way up.
4. **Flute casts (sole marks).** Elongate, tongue-shaped **scours cut in soft mud by a turbulent current**, with the deep rounded end facing upstream and the shallow end downstream; they are then filled by the sand deposited above, so that the **casts stand out on the underside (sole) of the overlying sandstone bed**. They are common in turbidite sequences, indicate the current direction and show which side was the base.
5. **Load casts and flame structures** (or **convolute bedding**). When sand is deposited quickly on water-saturated mud, the denser sand sinks into the mud as **rounded bulges (load casts)** at the base of the sand bed, and the mud is pushed up in tongues like flames (**flame structures**). These **soft-sediment deformation structures** are formed during or just after deposition, and also show the way up.

(Other correct examples are parallel lamination, bedding planes, groove casts, desiccation (mud) cracks, rain-drop prints and slump structures.) A neat sketch of each structure, labelled, is credited.
